source.version_note: Journal of Business Ethics, first online 10 June 2026, DOI 10.1007/s10551-026-06365-x; no issue locator supplied in Crossref metadata at verification.
source.verification_method: All sixteen pages read, including footnotes, sample exclusions, five models and references. Tables 1–4 at PDF pages 8–11 visually inspected. Crossref verifies article identity/date and two bibliography corrections. Chi-square tail checks use the printed values, not a raw-data reproduction.

citation.title: The Impact of ChatGPT’s Advice on Professional Judgment Related with Accounting and the Role of Accounting Education
citation.venue: Journal of Business Ethics, online 10 June 2026

reading.source_scope_note: One randomized advice-vignette study of Japanese accounting students, with substantial post-assignment exclusions and measured credibility/familiarity. Algorithmic authority and institutional isomorphism are proposed interpretations, not independently measured cognitive mechanisms. A binary consolidation choice is not a complete moral orientation or validation of professional accounting advice.
access_limits: Entire supplied PDF, tables and footnotes read. Full supplementary message wording, prompts, complete ChatGPT sessions and raw data are not embedded and were not independently inspected.

Data are not public and may require author request and ethics approval; no external contact was made. Cited monographs, original institutional-theory sources, professional codes and prior experiments were not fully read through this review.

study.sample: July 2025 survey at seven Japanese universities. 651 initial responses minus 28 incomplete, 99 I-don't-know judgments and 134 incorrect perceived-financial-impact answers yields 390 analyzed (59.91% retained). Mean age 20.35, 190 female, 196 male, four others; primarily second/third-year students, not practicing financial controllers.
study.assignment: Random assignment to no advice n=73, GenAI-deontological n=81, GenAI-consequential n=81, human-deontological n=78 and human-consequential n=77 after exclusions. Source is labeled ChatGPT-4o or a human auditor who is the recipient's friend. Human and AI content is held the same within framing, but friendship/expertise cues differ from the AI role prompt.
study.advice_content: GenAI material generated with ChatGPT-4o accessed 1 January 2025, prompted as an auditor. Both consequential conditions retain the original consolidation/deontological recommendation and append strategic arguments for nonconsolidation. This is additional mixed commentary, not an equally strong opposing-only recommendation or mere presence-of-content-neutral-advice manipulation.
study.outcome: Binary choice to consolidate company Y into X's statements. Authors label consolidation deontological and nonconsolidation consequential/aggressive. The latter serves favorable reported company results and covenant compliance, not necessarily overall social welfare; choosing it does not uniquely reveal a utilitarian philosophy, intention to mislead or actual misconduct.
study.covariates: Self-rated consolidation familiarity KNOW, binary internship INTER and one-item post-advice credibility CRED. CRED is available only to 317 advice recipients. AI credibility dichotomized 1–4 low n=67 versus 5–7 high n=95. High absolute credibility is not by itself comparative algorithm appreciation.
study.model1: Adjusted odds ratios relative to no advice: AI rules-based 2.89 [1.48,5.66], AI mixed 2.90 [1.47,5.71], human rules-based 3.98 [1.95,8.11], human mixed 2.28 [1.17,4.42]. KNOW OR1.19, p=.03; INTER OR.99, p=.98. These estimate selected-sample vignette choice, not universal advice-induced deontology or clinical/professional performance.
study.credibility: AI high-vs-low CRED OR2.08 [1.00,4.32], reported p=.05, a borderline measured association. Combined-source model CRED OR1.22 [1.01,1.47]; rules-only model1.44 [1.11,1.88]; mixed-advice .95 [.72,1.25], nonsignificant. No randomized credibility intervention, formal mediation test or source-independent causal pathway is identified.
study.source_comparison: Combined AI-versus-human OR.96 [.58,1.59]; rules context1.18 [.59,2.52]; mixed context .80 [.39,1.63], all nonsignificant. Wide intervals and no equivalence margins do not establish equal influence or prove source never matters. Controlling for post-advice CRED can also change the estimand relative to the total source effect.
study.education: KNOW associates with consolidation in most models except rules-only; this is self-rated familiarity, not tested knowledge or randomized teaching. INTER is nonsignificant in main/combined models and only marginal at .10 in mixed-advice (OR1.87 [.89,3.92], Wald 2.77). Ethics-course attendance is nonsignificant in all reported sensitivity checks. No demonstrated causal training or internship effect.
study.theory_scope: Institutional authority, mimetic/normative isomorphism and System1/System2 account for hypotheses but are not separately operationalized. No process timing, cognitive load manipulation, neural measure or imitation mechanism test supports assigning a cognitive system to a choice.

summary: Add algorithmic authority, mimetic isomorphism and aggressive financial reporting with perception/theory/domain-specific scope. Strengthen epistemic-trust context while separating absolute credibility from comparative algorithm appreciation, and alternative argument generation from proven post-hoc rationalization.

findings.definition: Treating an algorithmic system as a credible or legitimate source for deciding what information to accept or how to act.
findings.origin: Information studies / institutional and human–AI trust research
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit concept used to interpret advice-framing results; authority itself is not separately measured or randomized and comparative preference is not established
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether users or downstream agents accept recommendations because of an AI label, apparent professional role or verified evidence. Keep content and expertise cues matched, measure appropriate reliance and error detection, disclose actual provenance and preserve authorization. A system's confident professional persona must not be presented as a credential or authority to decide for affected people.
findings.novelty_rationale: Perceived authority/legitimacy can guide judgment without a direct command, evidence of uncritical error or a preference over humans. It therefore differs from obedience, automation bias and comparative algorithm appreciation, although these can interact.

evidence.quote: the trust placed in algorithms to
guide human decisions and verify information

findings.evidence_scope: The article explicitly defines algorithmic authority through secondary information-studies sources. AI advice conditions increase consolidation odds relative to no advice in the retained sample, and measured credibility is associated with choice in some models. These observations do not uniquely establish authority as mediator or show that the AI deserved trust.
findings.boundary: Legitimate reliance requires task-specific competence, evidence, lawful role and accountability. Algorithmic authority is not necessarily unwarranted, but an AI label or generated expert persona does not confer professional accreditation. High absolute credibility does not prove preference over humans or excuse bypassing independent scrutiny.

findings.definition: Adopting another actor's practices because they are perceived as successful, appropriate or legitimate, particularly under uncertainty.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Named theoretical imitation mechanism applied to individual advice use; this experiment does not directly identify institutional imitation or distinguish it from other advice effects
findings.ai_proposal: Audit whether an agent or organization copies a prominent model's policy, workflow or claimed best practice because it appears legitimate rather than because its suitability was checked. Compare evidence-backed adoption with copying after prestige or success cues, and assess local constraints. Retain beneficial transfer where supported; do not label all imitation or standardization a failure.
findings.novelty_rationale: Institutional copying of perceived legitimate/successful practices differs from aligning with a numerical majority, obeying a command or internalizing professional norms. It need not be mistaken and can occur without deliberate pressure; the original institutional theory is secondary here.

evidence.quote: mimetic isomorphism, where actors copy actions

findings.evidence_scope: The article explicitly names and explains mimetic isomorphism, then interprets advice use through it. No organizational diffusion data, legitimacy manipulation or independent imitation measure demonstrates this mechanism in the present student experiment; do not treat credibility correlations as a direct test of the full theory.
findings.boundary: Copying a demonstrably suitable practice can be rational. Institutional imitation, majority conformity, professional socialization and AI training-data imitation are different processes. One matching answer or borrowed practice does not establish the motive, social mechanism or a model's subjective desire for legitimacy.

findings.definition: Presenting financial events favorably through reporting positions that are not clearly supported by the facts or applicable professional standards.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary definition and student binary-decision proxy in one hypothetical consolidation scenario; no actual reporting misconduct, deceptive intent or AI behavior independently verified
findings.ai_proposal: Review AI-assisted financial narratives and calculations for unsupported exclusion of losses, selective consolidation assumptions or favorable interpretations that conflict with evidence. Require traceable facts and applicable accounting review before consequential use. Separately test analogous selective project/evaluation reporting rather than silently calling every favorable summary financial misconduct.
findings.novelty_rationale: A domain-specific reporting practice differs from merely optimistic wording or knowingly lying: ambiguous or unsupported favorable accounting choices can be aggressive without proven deception. The accounting construct is explicitly defined; legitimate discretion must remain distinguished from the questionable practice.

evidence.quote: not clearly supported by the facts

findings.evidence_scope: The article cites Cuccia et al. for the definition and treats nonconsolidating a loss-making related entity as an aggressive choice in its designed scenario. No actual financial statements or professional participants are audited; the original definition paper and applicable current accounting standard were not independently reviewed.
findings.boundary: Favorable results, estimates, uncertainty or a lawful judgment call do not automatically imply aggressive reporting, fraud or bad intent. Establish relevant facts, control conditions and professional requirements. A binary student choice cannot diagnose a moral philosophy or authorize a legal/financial conclusion about a real entity.

findings.definition: Trust in another source as a provider of reliable knowledge or guidance.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds context on one-item advice credibility and its framing-dependent association with judgment, not a new synonym for trust.

evidence.quote: you find the advice you received?

findings.evidence_scope: CRED asks perceived credibility of the advice received. Positive associations appear in combined/rules-based models but not mixed-advice. This is a measured informational appraisal, not a validated general epistemic-trust trait, clinical epistemic trust or proof of appropriate calibration.
findings.boundary: Credibility after a decision can reflect agreement, source cues or rationalization; temporal and causal direction remain uncertain. A one-item credibility score is not an independent finding that advice is true, and its association does not establish a training or trust-building intervention.

findings.definition: Giving greater weight or preference to algorithmic advice or judgment than to human advice or judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Prevents the paper's absolute AI-credibility high/low grouping from silently replacing the comparative construct.

evidence.quote: defined as perceiving advice from GenAI as highly credible

findings.evidence_scope: The authors label high AI credibility algorithm appreciation. Model 2 compares high versus low credibility within AI recipients, not AI-versus-human advice weight or preference. Direct source comparisons are nonsignificant with wide intervals. Boundary-only coverage, not a fresh demonstrated appreciation effect.
findings.boundary: Finding one AI message credible does not establish preference for algorithms over people. The 2019 Logg paper cannot be treated as a direct ChatGPT test simply because this 2026 article uses ChatGPT as a contemporary example.

findings.definition: Constructing reasons after a judgment or reaction to justify it, rather than those reasons necessarily having produced it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinguishes generating prompted alternative strategic arguments from proving that a model's explanation misrepresents the causes of its prior judgment.

evidence.quote: when further prompted for alternative perspectives

findings.evidence_scope: The authors report ChatGPT producing additional justifications for an alternative after an initial recommendation. Full prompts/traces are not embedded, and no causal-faithfulness or deliberation study tests whether these are confabulated reasons rather than requested alternatives. Boundary-only note.
findings.boundary: Considering a legitimate alternative is not itself rationalization or deception. The issue is whether reasons are accurately represented, supported and relevant, not whether a system can discuss competing arguments.

methodological_limits: Students from one country and one accounting vignette are proxies, not financial controllers or auditors working under real stakes. No actual professional performance, fraud, educational gain or present-day model capability is measured.

Forty percent of initial responses are excluded. Removing 99 I-don't-know judgments selects on an uncertainty response closely related to the outcome, not merely attention. Exclusions after advice can disrupt randomization if conditions affect understanding or decisiveness; original condition-specific attrition and intention-to-treat sensitivity are not supplied.

The binary outcome maps one scenario's consolidation choice to deontology/consequentialism. A choice may reflect technical interpretation, uncertainty, incentives or misunderstanding rather than a stable moral theory. Favoring one company's ratios is not equivalent to maximizing overall welfare; deontology is not the only normative ethical theory.

Both consequential conditions retain the initial deontological recommendation and append strategic commentary. This bundles framing, length and conflicting arguments; it does not show advice overrides an equally strong contrary recommendation or that mere source presence independently induces deontology.

The human source is a friend who is an auditor; the AI is role-prompted as an auditor. Same written content does not match professional accreditation, interpersonal relationship or expertise expectations. A generated persona is not an actual licensed professional.

Credibility, familiarity and internship are measured rather than randomized. Post-advice credibility can be affected by the treatment or outcome; adjusting for it does not cleanly identify a total source effect and may introduce selection/confounding. No formal causal mediation test supports calling credibility a common mediator.

High versus low CRED is a dichotomy of one absolute credibility item, not a comparative algorithm-appreciation scale. Borderline Model 2 Wald 3.89 p≈.0486/printed .05 and rounded CI[1, 4.32] do not warrant a strong trait or causal claim.

Nonsignificant source effects with broad CIs do not establish equivalence, identical mechanisms or no role of advisor source. No prespecified equivalence margin or source × framing interaction test is reported; different subgroup significance patterns are not an interaction test.

KNOW is self-rated familiarity rather than objective tested knowledge, and internship participation is self-selected. INTER is nonsignificant in main/combined models, only marginal at .10 in the mixed-advice subgroup with 95% CI including one. Ethics-course attendance is nonsignificant in all five sensitivity checks. Avoid the abstract's broad causal implication that accounting education or internships protect judgment.

System1/System2 and institutional imitation are explanatory hypotheses. No response-time, cognitive-process, manipulation of professional norms, neural or emotional measurement identifies them. A deontological decision is not inherently intuitive and a consequential decision not inherently more deliberative.

Printed model degrees of freedom and significance summaries conflict. Model 2 table gives χ²9.04 df3 (p≈.0288), prose df4 (p≈.0601). Model 3 table gives χ²9.07 df4 (p≈.0594), prose df3 (p≈.0284) and says 1% while also writing p<.05. These alternatives cannot all be correct; fit output is required.

Model 4 χ²9.48 df4 implies p≈.05016, slightly above .05 despite a significant .05 label/prose. Rounding the statistic to two decimals does not support a strict p<.05 assertion here. The coefficient-level CRED result is a distinct test and is not erased by this omnibus discrepancy.

Model 2 INTER Wald 2.29 with one df implies p≈.1302 rather than .22; both are nonsignificant at .05. Model 5 INTER Wald 2.77 implies p≈.0960, consistent with a marginal .10 label, not conventional .05 significance. Do not silently strengthen the internship conclusion.

Model 1 accuracy 68.5% is only about 1.1 percentage points above always choosing the majority nonconsolidation outcome (263/390=67.44%). Classification accuracy is not a moral-quality measure or robust prediction evaluation. No held-out validation or class-specific errors are supplied.

Odds ratios describe odds, not probability multipliers or percentage-point increases. Familiarity OR1.19 and credibility OR1.22 do not mean a person's consolidation probability necessarily rises 19% or 22%. Baseline probabilities, intercepts and condition counts would be needed for absolute effects.

University-affiliation/type and ethics-course sensitivity statements are useful but detailed fitted tables and coding are not supplied. Treating university affiliation as one covariate may depend on coding; these checks do not by themselves demonstrate clustered or multi-level uncertainty handling.

CRED inclusion is described inconsistently: one passage says only Models 4/5, while Table 3 explicitly groups by CRED and Model 3 includes it. Use the displayed model specifications rather than the oversimplified summary.

Some 2022/2019 background descriptions refer to ChatGPT even though the cited research predates this study's ChatGPT-4o materials. Do not attribute a specific modern model test to an older generic algorithm study without reading that original source.

Current professional codes, Japanese standards, ISO documents and actual consolidation requirements have not been independently audited. The source's scenario interpretation is not a financial/legal recommendation, and normative correctness requires more than copying its binary label.

Five regression models and several subgroup/sensitivity analyses are one study/article, not five independent research papers. Data and complete messages are unavailable here; reported numeric conflicts remain unresolved rather than guessed away.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Source credibility and actual provenance must be kept separate. A rule-based agent believed to represent doctors and ChatGPT role-prompted as an auditor can both acquire perceived authority without genuine professional credentials; neither observation alone identifies blind obedience.

A self-reported appraisal can predict another judgment without identifying the underlying reasoning or its moral correctness. Absolute credibility is not comparative preference, just as fairness-property reports are not verified causal properties.

Predicting or encouraging a preferred normative label is not establishing morality. Binary accounting labels, like Delphi crowd labels, require an explicit normative and domain-validity argument before being used as ethical ground truth.

Check all coefficients, design contrasts and fit statistics before accepting a summary. The taxi paper's total-effect conflict and this paper's df/p/education discrepancies limit causal slogans while leaving clearly defined concepts usable with narrower scope.

deferred.reason: Professional socialization mechanism named in a theoretical footnote, not independently tested. Keep distinct from mimetic copying and avoid adding the entire institutional-theory taxonomy based only on this secondary application.

Broad normative/cognitive approaches, not uniquely identified by one consolidation choice. Existing moral reasoning entries retain context; self-interested reporting is not automatically utilitarianism.
One-item measured credibility, selected sample and no formal causal mediation prevent treating this as a new established mechanism or general AI effect.

Familiarity and internships are not randomized, internship evidence is largely null/marginal, and ethics-course attendance is null. No proven new protective training behavior or guaranteed intervention follows.

deferred.term: AI consequentialist bias / AI normative authority transfer
deferred.reason: Generated/adapted messages in one study do not establish intrinsic model values. Authority transfer is a theoretical interpretation already represented by algorithmic authority, not a second proven effect.

limitations: Three perception/theory/domain-specific concepts added, with no assertion of professional performance, broad moral superiority, clinical/legal/financial advice or new automatic normative links. Two boundary-only sources do not inflate comparative-appreciation or rationalization paper coverage.
